Movement Along and Shift of AS
IAL 2.3.3 · 1b and 1c: the upward-sloping SRAS curve, a movement along it when the price level changes, a shift when costs change, and a movement along a vertical LRAS that leaves output unchanged.
A movement along the SRAS curve
Same curve: only the price level changed.
Price level on the vertical axis, real national output on the horizontal
A movement along SRAS from $800bn at 100 to $820bn at 104
A shift to SRAS₁, drawn as a new labelled curve, supplying $775bn at 100
On a vertical LRAS, a change in the price level with output unchanged
A shift of the SRAS curve
A new curve: firms supply less at every price level.
A movement along a vertical LRAS
Only a shift of LRAS changes long-run output.

IAL 2.3.3 · 2a: a change in the costs of raw materials and energy, in the exchange rate and in tax rates, each moving the SRAS curve through unit costs.
The original SRAS and the new SRAS₁ both drawn and labelled
The direction of the shift shown with an arrow at an unchanged price level
Energy 25% of costs × 20% = unit costs up 5%
A depreciation shifting SRAS left, an appreciation shifting it right
Imported inputs 10% dearer: unit costs up 3%.
Imported inputs cheaper: unit costs down 3%.
Tax adds 2% to the cost of each unit.

IAL 2.3.3 · 3a: the classical LRAS, vertical at capacity, with the adjustment that returns output there after AD falls — AD, SRAS and LRAS on one diagram — and the Keynesian LRAS with its three ranges.
The classical LRAS: vertical at capacity
A vertical classical LRAS at capacity, $800bn
After AD falls: the short-run point $770bn at 94, then SRAS₁ and the long-run point at 88
The Keynesian curve with three named ranges: flat, rising, vertical
Both curves vertical at the same capacity
AD falls $60bn: short run, then long run
Short run: $770bn at 94. Wages fall; SRAS right.
Long run: back to $800bn, price level 88.
Vertical at $800bn: every resource in use.
Long-Run AS: Technology, Productivity and Skills
Before the next chapter: the diagram, a quick question and one thing from earlier.
IAL 2.3.3 · 3b: technology, productivity and education and skills each raise output per worker, so capacity rises and the LRAS curve shifts right.
The original LRAS and the new LRAS₁ both vertical and labelled
Capacity = labour force × output per worker: 40 million × $20,000 = $800bn
Technology: $840bn; more machinery per worker: $824bn; training: $816bn
No extra workers, more from each.
Arrives only once the trained are at work.
Long-Run AS: Regulation, Population and Competition
Before you finish: the diagram, a quick question and one thing from earlier.
IAL 2.3.3 · 3b: an ageing population, a rise in participation and a net inflow of migrants each change the number of workers, so capacity and the LRAS curve move.
Ageing: 1 million fewer of working age
Labour force = working-age population × participation: 50 million × 80% = 40 million
Higher participation: $820bn; a net inflow of migrants: $830bn
The same population, more of it at work.
Immigration minus emigration, all at work.
